column4: The section's ع ط و note derives giving from reaching by hand; Moses says God “gave each thing its creation, then guided it” (أعطى … هدى), making guidance follow the gift of a fitting nature.
The section joins the asker, God's giving, and His نعمة; here God gives what people سألتموه and His نعمة cannot be counted, placing request, answer, and unmeasurable favor together.
The section pictures the Lord's hand as giver; this ayah says bounty is بيد الله and He gives it to whom He wills, locating both the gift and its choice with God.
The section names عطاء as a gift; this ayah calls provision for both groups عطاء ربك and says it is not withheld, showing the breadth of that divine giving.
The section's ع ط و root is used directly in أعطيناك: God gives the Prophet al-Kawthar, an explicit instance of the promised hand reaching its recipient.
The section's root note for عطو meets the afterlife's عطاء غير مجذوذ, a gift “unsevered”; it makes the promised giving endure.
Sulayman calls his grant هذا عطاؤنا and may give or hold it (أمسك); the same giving root makes visible a recipient's choice over what has been entrusted to him.
This is the section's stated example of the giver: the one who أعطى and is mindful. It places human giving alongside the Lord's gift in 93:5.
The section's ه د ي note links guidance with a gift; the Queen says she will send a هدية, making that root's material gift sense concrete.
After the Queen's هدية in 27:35, Solomon asks if they supply him wealth and says what God آتاني is better than theirs; his answer separates a human gift from God's greater grant.
The section's hand passes or receives a gift; this command says not to bind one's hand to one's neck or open it fully (ولا تبسطها كل البسط), giving the image a measure between withholding and excess.
The section shows a hand giving and a hand that may hold; here what God opens of mercy no one can withhold, and what He withholds no one can send after, making Him the final giver and holder.
The section pictures the giving hand; this ayah says خير is in God's hand and He gives and takes away sovereignty, joining bounty to God's power to grant or remove.
The section's upward-giving hand belongs to God; this ayah says no one controls His فضل and that bounty is in His hand, a boundary against treating the gift as human property.
The section's generous hand still gives according to need; here God says He would let provision overflow if He did, but sends it down by measure, explaining restraint as deliberate measure.
The section sets the Hereafter as better than the first life; this ayah says God expands or restricts provision and contrasts rejoicing in this life with its small share against the Hereafter.
The section's claim that the Hereafter is better than the first life is restated as “the Hereafter is better and more enduring” (والآخرة خير وأبقى), extending the contrast to permanence.
The section's خير of the Hereafter is set against gifts in this life; here what people are given is only its enjoyment, while what is with God is خير وأبقى.
Following the hand measure in 17:29, this ayah says the Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it; the neighbor turns the human rule of measured giving toward God's provision.
The section's hand should not be wholly closed or flung open; this ayah describes the faithful as spending neither extravagantly nor stingily, but in a middle course.
The section warns against a closed hand; this ayah condemns those who withhold what God gave them (بما آتاهم الله من فضله), saying it will become a collar around their necks.
This begins the passage completed in 9:76: people promise to give charity if God grants them bounty, making their request and intended return explicit.
It completes 9:75: after God gives them from His bounty, they withhold and turn away, a direct reversal of the open hand and the sâ'il's hope.
The section's giver transfers a gift; here a God-fearing person يوتي ماله to purify himself, making human giving a response to the divine gift.
The section's grant ends with satisfaction (فترضى); at the end of the giving passage begun in 92:18, the giver too “will be satisfied” (ولسوف يرضى), linking giving with contentment.
The section's open-palmed سائل is not a nuisance: this ayah says there is a right in the believers' wealth for the سائل and the deprived.
The section's asker appears here as a defined claim: the faithful keep a known حق in their wealth, which 70:25 identifies for the asker and deprived.
This neighbor specifies the right named in 70:24 as belonging to the سائل and the deprived, giving the section's asker a place in the giver's wealth.
The section's gift and asker meet in the definition of righteousness: a person gives wealth from love to relatives, orphans, needy people, travelers, and السائلين.
Asked what to spend, the answer names خير and directs it to parents, kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers; the section's “gift” sense of خير meets actual giving to recipients.
This ayah names poor people who do not ask others persistently (لا يسألون الناس إلحافا); it lets the reader see the needy who may not appear as the section's audible sâ'il.
The section's سائل asks for a gift; this ayah widens the scene to all in heaven and earth يسأله, with God continually acting as the one turned to.

The section's سâ'il asks a human not to rebuke him; here people ask the Prophet about God, who answers that He is near and responds to the caller, distinguishing a divine answer from a human's duty to give.
The disciples ask Jesus whether his Lord can send down a table from heaven; this begins a passage in which petitioners seek a gift from above, close to the section's ask-and-give movement.
The disciples explain in 5:112 that they want to eat from the table and reassure their hearts; their stated need makes the requested heavenly gift more than a spectacle.
Jesus asks for the table as a feast and sign and says “provide for us”; this neighbor gives the heavenly gift a communal and provisionary purpose.
God answers the request in 5:112–114 by promising to send the table down, then warns those who disbelieve afterward; the grant from above carries a boundary of responsibility.
The section forbids the hand that takes from an orphan without consent; this ayah says those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly fill their bellies with fire.
The section forbids taking from the orphan; this command says to give orphans their property and not consume it with one's own, setting the exact boundary on the hand.
The section's forbidden reach over the orphan is answered by testing orphans until maturity and handing their property back (فادفعوا إليهم أموالهم), rather than consuming it first.
The section forbids overpowering an orphan; this command forbids approaching the orphan's property except in the best way until maturity, protecting what the hand might take.
The command not to approach an orphan's property except in the best way echoes the section's ban on taking from the vulnerable and extends it to keeping the covenant.
The section forbids overpowering the orphan; this answer to a question about orphans says reforming their affairs is better and calls them brothers, shifting the hand from taking to care.
The section protects the orphan against a hand that seizes; Moses learns that the wall was repaired to preserve the treasure of two orphan boys until they grew, an act of protection from above.
The section forbids overpowering an orphan; this ruling calls for justice toward orphan girls and children, including those whose prescribed rights might be withheld.
The section tells the addressee not to qahr the orphan; this ayah exposes the denier of judgment as one who يدع اليتيم, driving the orphan away.
The section forbids humiliating the orphan; this rebuke says people fail to honor (لا تكرمون) the orphan, naming the social reversal of that command.
The same rebuke continues from 89:17: people do not urge one another to feed the poor, extending orphan neglect into refusal to provide.
The rebuke continues to devouring inheritance greedily; this gives a concrete picture of the unjust hand the section warns against.
The closing charge of this sequence is intense love of wealth; beside the orphan's neglected claim in 89:17–19, it shows what the grasping hand serves.
The section names the orphan and the asker among vulnerable recipients; here the righteous give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving it.
This neighbor explains the feeding in 76:8: the givers seek God's face and desire neither repayment nor thanks, making the gift free of a claim on its recipient.
The section's care for a vulnerable recipient is staged as feeding during famine; the next verses specify an orphan near at hand and then a destitute person.
This neighbor specifies one recipient of the famine feeding in 90:14 as an orphan who is a close relative.
This neighbor adds the poor person in the dust to the famine scene begun in 90:14, showing another recipient of the extended hand.
When orphans, kin, and poor people are present at inheritance division, this command says to give them something and speak kindly; it joins the section's hand-gift to its concern with words.
This command says to give relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due; it gives the section's reaching hand a concrete list of people to serve.
The neighbor to the gift command in 17:26 calls spendthrifts brothers of devils; it bounds generosity against waste, like the section's warning against opening the hand fully.
If one must turn away from the needy because one seeks mercy from the Lord, this neighbor commands a gentle word; it directly answers the section's ban on rebuking the asker.
The section moves from God's gift to speaking of it; this ayah says not to follow a charitable gift with reminders or injury, guarding the recipient from a hurtful word.
This neighbor says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, making speech to a requester part of giving well.
It warns that charity is voided by reminders and injury; the section's report of God's gift is thus distinct from using one's gift to shame its recipient.
This ayah weighs making charity visible against concealing it and giving to the poor; it complicates the section's public telling of God's favor with a distinction about human alms.
This neighbor gives the secret/public dimension of spending: believers give by night and day, privately and openly, and have their reward with their Lord.
The section's hand carries a gift to another; this command says to spend from good things earned and grown, not to choose bad goods one would not accept oneself.
The section's gift is a form of خير; this ayah says righteousness is not reached until one spends from what one loves, then calls whatever is spent خير.
The section's Lord gives and human hands transfer; this command tells believers to give enslaved people from God's wealth that He has given them.
This command tells the addressee to give a relative, poor person, and traveler their due; it turns the section's open hand into directed generosity.
The section's gifts pass between hands; here God promises to replace what people spend, naming Him the best provider and completing the transfer with return.
The section shows giving and receiving; this ayah asks who will lend God a goodly loan, which He multiplies, turning a human gift into a promised divine return.
This command says to give women their bridal gifts graciously (نحلة); it makes a hand-to-hand transfer depend on honoring the recipient.
After describing a substantial gift to a wife, this ayah forbids taking any of it back; it directly bounds the section's branch of reaching for what is not one's right.
This neighbor gives the reason for the rule in 4:20: the spouses have been intimate and taken a solemn covenant from one another, placing a moral boundary on reclaiming a gift.
The section's dark ع ط و branch is taking what one has no right to; this command forbids consuming one another's wealth wrongfully and allows trade by mutual consent.
The section names improper reaching for another's due; this ayah forbids consuming people's wealth wrongfully or using it to influence judges.
The section's unauthorized hand reaches for another's property; this ayah forbids taking back what was given to wives, with the stated exception of an agreed ransom when the limits are feared.
The section's ع ط و note includes taking what is not rightfully yours; the theft ruling treats unlawful taking as a hand-action with a legal boundary.
The section names taʿāṭī as taking what is not one's right; in the she-camel scene one man فتعاطى ثم عقر, so the shared root becomes a destructive reach.
The section glosses قهر as dominance and taking from above; here God is القاهر فوق عباده, a sovereign use of the same above/dominance image that contrasts with human oppression of an orphan.
The same قاهر فوق عباده formula appears before God's messengers take each person at death; its context makes the section's “from above” power divine custody, unlike the forbidden human grasp.
Pharaoh's people claim إنا فوقهم قاهرون over the Israelites; this boast stages the abusive domination from above that the section forbids toward a vulnerable orphan.
The section praises the one who gives; the paired warning begins with whoever withholds (بخل) and thinks himself self-sufficient, the reversed hand in the previous surah.
This ayah sets the people of the Fire in painful permanence; its neighbor 11:108 names the contrasting Paradise gift as عطاء غير مجذوذ, clarifying what “unsevered gift” answers.
The section connects هدى with a gift; here God promises guidance from Him and says whoever follows هداي will have no fear, presenting guidance as a granted path with a response.
The section's ه د ي note draws a gift sense from guidance; this ayah says the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves, but God guides whom He wills, locating that guidance with the giver.
The saved people say الحمد لله الذي هدانا لهذا; their spoken praise for God's guidance concretely joins the section's guided recipient to its command to speak of the Lord's favor.
After recognizing the ant's speech, Solomon asks God to enable him to thank His نعمة; this makes the section's received favor lead to words addressed back to its giver.
The section ends with telling God's نعمة; this promise says gratitude for a favor brings increase, connecting acknowledgment with further giving.
The section calls نعمة a hand and favor; this ayah says that if people tried to count God's نعمة they could not number them, like 14:34's uncountable blessing.
The section tells the Prophet to speak of the Lord's نعمة; this command to eat God's provision and be grateful for His favor supplies a direct response to receiving.
The section's transfer of a gift has a reciprocal form here: whoever lends God a goodly loan will have it multiplied many times, so giving is pictured as entrusted value returned by God.
The section's خير can name a gift; this ayah says whatever good people spend is for themselves and will be repaid, joining خير to material giving.
The section's gift is a transfer whose reach can grow; this parable makes money spent in God's path like a grain multiplied into many ears, showing divine increase after giving.
Moses asks God for whatever خير He sends down because he is in need; the section's asker becomes a prayerful recipient awaiting provision.
This neighbor answers Moses' need in 28:24: one of the women invites him to her father to be paid for watering their flock, turning a request for خير into a human exchange.
The section's gazelle reaches up for leaves; this ayah mentions trees in which people pasture their animals, a broader grazing scene that recalls the animal reaching for food.
The section's mihda is a platter that carries a gift; this scene has gold platters and cups carried around in Paradise, a plausible but uncertain parallel in serving vessels.
The section says the Hereafter is better than the first life; this ayah contrasts worldly wealth and children with lasting good works, a related but less direct account of what remains.
The section's lexical example is an animal reaching for leaves; this ayah names provision for people and their livestock after pasture, a broad animal-feeding parallel without the reaching gesture.
